newsitem.title: USA: Democrats have momentum in U.S. Congress elections.
newsitem.headline: Democrats have momentum in U.S. Congress elections.

text.p: Less than three weeks before the Nov. 5 election, momentum has swung to Democrats in Congressional elections and could propel them to a majority in the U.S. House of Representatives, political experts said.
But the odds are that Republicans will retain a majority in the Senate, they predicted.
"Either Democrats come just short of taking back the House or they take it back," predicted Elizabeth Wilner, who covers the House for the Cook Political Report.

House Republicans now hold a 235-198 majority. Democrats need a net gain of 18 seats to take back control of the House. They recently took one Republican seat in Louisiana, and Democrats have the support of the lone independent member of Congress.

In the Senate, where Republicans hold a 53-47 majority, Democrats need a three seat gain to be even with Republicans. If President Bill Clinton is reelected, Democrat Vice President Al Gore could cast a Senate vote to break any tie.

Earlier this year, both sides assumed Republicans would keep the majorities in both chambers they won in the 1994 election. But experts say Clinton's dominance of the presidential race could become a landslide that sweeps in a Democratic House.
"I think there's a pretty good chance that will happen," said Ruy Teixeira, an expert on voter turnout. "That's the (Republican) nightmare."
Teixeira believes if Clinton wins by 10 to 12 percentage points, his coattails will pull in a Democratic House majority. Reuters pollster John Zogby puts the crucial margin at 13 percent.

"When the Clinton lead hits 13 percent, that spills over into the questions 'which party would you prefer as the majority in the House and Senate?'" Zogby said. "Those two questions tip over onto the Democratic side."
The Reuters tracking poll on Saturday showed Clinton losing a bit of his lead to Dole. The Saturday poll put Clinton ahead by 7.8 percent, down from 9.0 percent on Friday.
But Zogby said that after the previous presidential debate Dole also gained, only to later fall back.
The Saturday Zogby poll showed voters picked Republicans for the House over Democrats by 41.5 percent to 37.5, a margin of four percentage points, up substantially from Friday's margin of 0.8.
In the Senate, Republicans were ahead 42.7 percent to 37.4, or 5.3 percent, up from Friday's margin of 3.2.
But a widened Clinton lead would shift votes to the Democratic side, Zogby said.

Although the key factor in Democratic momentum is Clinton's popularity, another reason is strong backing from their traditional allies in the trade union movement, who have been working for months to topple the Republicans.

The AFL-CIO union has run ads linking Republicans to the unpopular House Speaker Newt Gingrich. In district after district, the ads highlight votes in support of Gingrich policies, blaming Republicans for two government shutdowns and changes in Medicare the ads say will hurt senior citizens.
Experts said the election could turn on how the huge freshman class of 73 Republicans elected in 1994 fare.

Wilner said the Democrats have fewer tight races than Republicans in House elections. Some 41 House races in Republican-held seats are considered too close to call, with most of those members of the freshman class. Five Democratic-held seats are leaning to the Republicans but only another 20 Democratic seats are considered too close to call.

But in the Senate elections, a Democratic victory is considered more of a long shot. To win control of the Senate, political analyst Charles Cook says Democrats must take all seven of the closest races -- in Massachusetts, Arkansas, New Jersey, South Dakota, New Hampshire, Maine and Oregon.

And Republicans have one big advantage over Democrats in the final two weeks of campaigning -- lots of money that will enable them to launch a round of television ads in states where tracking polls show Senate races neck-and-neck.
But Democrats hope the popular Clinton will blunt the money advantage by making last-minute campaign stops in states with close Congressional races.
